topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Which of the following is a weakness of the pure 'out-of-pocket' financing model?
o: Too much risk pooling
Excessive government control over hospitals
Compulsory contributions from employers
Absence of risk pooling, so illness costs fall entirely on the sick household at the time of need
e: OOP payment provides no pooling or prepayment, leading to catastrophic spending and foregone care; it is the dominant model in low-income settings.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: The Universal Health Insurance Scheme (UHIS) launched in 2003 by public sector insurers was designed for:
o: Central government employees
Corporate executives
Families below the poverty line with a government premium subsidy and a cover of ₹30,000
Overseas travellers
e: UHIS was a subsidised scheme for BPL families offering ₹30,000 hospitalisation cover; it had limited uptake and was later overshadowed by RSBY.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: In October 2024 PM-JAY was extended to cover which additional group irrespective of income?
o: All government employees
All students
All farmers
All citizens aged 70 years and above
e: The Ayushman Vay Vandana card extended PM-JAY's ₹5 lakh family cover to all senior citizens aged 70+, regardless of socio-economic status.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: In a 'trust mode' implementation of a State health assurance scheme:
o: A State-constituted agency or trust directly empanels hospitals and pays claims, bearing the risk itself
An insurer is paid a premium and bears the claims risk
Hospitals bear the risk through capitation
Beneficiaries pay premium to a trust
e: In trust mode the State retains the risk and pays providers; insurance mode transfers the risk to an insurer for a premium, and hybrid mode splits the two.

topic: Health Financing Models and Health Financing in India
t: Which of the following best describes the role of private health insurance in India's overall health financing?
o: It is the largest source of financing, exceeding government spending
It covers all hospital expenses for the entire population
It is a small but growing component, used mainly by the urban middle class and employer groups, while government spending and out-of-pocket payment dominate
It has been replaced entirely by PM-JAY
e: Commercial health insurance accounts for a modest share of total health expenditure; employer groups and urban retail customers form most of its base.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: A 'sub-limit' in a health insurance policy is:
o: The maximum the insurer pays for a specific expense head or procedure (e.g. room rent, cataract), within the overall sum insured
The minimum claim amount
The premium for a dependent
A reduction in waiting period
e: Sub-limits cap particular heads such as room rent or listed surgeries to control cost; they operate within, not in addition to, the sum insured.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: A 'disease-specific' or 'critical illness' product typically covers:
o: All hospitalisations of any kind
A defined list of serious illnesses such as cancer, heart attack, stroke, kidney failure and major organ transplant, paying a lump sum on diagnosis
Only OPD consultations
Only accidental injuries
e: CI products pay a benefit on first diagnosis of a listed condition meeting the policy definition, after any survival period; they do not reimburse bills.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: Mr Sinha holds an individual policy with sum insured ₹5 lakh and a deductible of ₹25,000 per claim. His admissible hospital bill is ₹1,25,000 and the policy has a 10% co-pay applied after the deductible. The insurer pays:
e: After the deductible, ₹1,25,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹1,00,000; applying 10% co-pay, the insurer pays 90% = ₹90,000.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: A pure premium of ₹4,000 is to be loaded for expenses of 25% and profit of 5% of gross premium. The gross premium is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). When loadings are expressed as a percentage of gross premium, gross = pure ÷ (1 − 0.25 − 0.05) = 4,000 ÷ 0.70 = ₹5,714 (approx.).

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: Which of the following statements about group health policies is correct?
o: Premium cannot vary from one group to another
Group policies are often customised with waived waiting periods, maternity and parental cover, and are priced on group experience
Group policies cannot provide cashless facility
Members cannot migrate to individual cover on leaving
e: Employer groups commonly negotiate waivers and extra benefits priced on claims experience; migration to individual policies on exit is mandated by IRDAI.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: A personal accident policy differs from a health indemnity policy in that it:
o: Covers illness-related hospitalisation only
Pays defined benefits for death or disablement caused by accident, typically as a multiple of annual income or a chosen capital sum
Requires a 36-month waiting period
Is sold only by life insurers
e: PA cover is benefit-based and accident-only, with benefit tables for death, permanent total/partial disablement and temporary total disablement; there are no disease waiting periods.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: The 'Mashak Rakshak' standard product was designed to cover:
o: Vector-borne diseases such as dengue, malaria and chikungunya on a benefit basis
COVID-19 hospitalisation
Cancer treatment
Accidental death
e: Mashak Rakshak (2021) is a standard vector-borne disease benefit cover; Corona Kavach/Rakshak covered COVID-19.

topic: Health Insurance Products in India
t: Which of the following is an incorrect statement about a family floater policy?
o: A single premium is charged for the family based on the age of the eldest member and the number of members
The sum insured can be used by any member, singly or jointly
It is usually cheaper than separate individual policies with the same total cover
Each member is guaranteed the full sum insured independently of claims by other members
e: In a floater the sum insured is shared, so claims by one member reduce what is available to others; the other statements are true.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: The proposal form in health insurance serves as:
o: The policy document itself
A receipt for premium
A claim form
The basis of the contract, containing the proposer's declarations on which the insurer assesses the risk
e: The proposal form carries material disclosures and the declaration of truth; the policy is issued on its basis and misstatements can affect claims.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: Which of the following is a lifestyle factor relevant to health underwriting?
o: The proposer's mother tongue
The proposer's bank
Consumption of alcohol and tobacco
Number of previous insurers
e: Alcohol and tobacco use are strongly associated with morbidity and are routinely asked about; the other factors have no bearing on health risk.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Under the IRDAI Master Circular on health insurance (2024), after how many months of continuous coverage can an insurer no longer contest a claim on grounds of non-disclosure or misrepresentation, except for established fraud?
o: 36 months
48 months
60 months
96 months
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The moratorium period was reduced from 8 years (96 months) to 60 months in 2024; after it, claims can be contested only for proven fraud or for permanent exclusions.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: A 58-year-old proposer discloses that she underwent angioplasty two years ago. The underwriter is most likely to:
o: Treat heart disease as a pre-existing disease, and consider a loading plus waiting period or a specific exclusion for cardiac conditions, or decline depending on severity
Accept at standard rates
Issue the policy with no waiting period because the procedure is complete
Refer the case to the Ombudsman
e: Coronary artery disease with intervention is a significant PED; underwriting response depends on severity and time elapsed, ranging from loaded acceptance with exclusions to decline.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: 'Tele-underwriting' in health insurance refers to:
o: Underwriting done by the television advertising team
Collecting health information from the proposer through a structured telephone or video interview by trained personnel, often recorded
Underwriting overseas risks
Underwriting only group policies
e: Tele-underwriting improves disclosure quality and reduces agent-influenced non-disclosure; the recorded call forms part of the underwriting record.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: Which of the following statements about underwriting of a health policy for a child is correct?
o: Children cannot be covered under health insurance
Children are generally covered as dependents under a parent's policy, with insurers specifying minimum entry ages (e.g. 90 days or 3 months) and requiring at least one adult to be insured
Children must undergo full medical examination
Children are charged the same premium as senior citizens
e: Dependent children are added from a minimum age set by the product; medical tests are not normally required and premiums are low reflecting lower morbidity.

topic: Health Insurance Underwriting
t: An insurer decides that a proposer with a disclosed history of kidney stones five years ago, with no recurrence, will be accepted with a 24-month exclusion for urinary tract calculi. This decision is an example of:
o: Declinature
Community rating
Accepting with a specific waiting period/exclusion to manage a known but moderate risk
Postponement
e: A time-bound specific exclusion allows cover while protecting the pool from a likely early claim; postponement would have deferred the decision and declinature would have refused cover.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: A policy's 'operative clause' or insuring clause sets out:
o: The names of network hospitals
The grievance redressal procedure
The list of non-payable items
The insurer's promise to pay, subject to the terms, conditions and exclusions, in consideration of the premium
e: The operative clause is the core promise of the contract; schedules, conditions and exclusions elaborate and limit it.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Which of the following is a correct statement about the standard exclusion for maternity (Excl18)?
o: Medical expenses related to pregnancy and childbirth are excluded unless specifically covered, but ectopic pregnancy is treated as an exception
Maternity can never be covered under any health policy
Maternity is covered without waiting period in all policies
Maternity exclusion applies only to men
e: Standard maternity exclusion carves out ectopic pregnancy as covered; insurers may offer maternity as an optional benefit with a waiting period.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: The 'disclosure to information norm' in a health policy states that:
o: The policy is void only if a claim is fraudulent
The insurer must disclose its profit to the insured
The hospital must disclose its tariff
The policy shall be void and all premium forfeited in the event of misrepresentation, mis-description or non-disclosure of any material fact, subject to the moratorium provision
e: This clause operationalises utmost good faith; however, after the 60-month moratorium, non-disclosure cannot be invoked except for proven fraud.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Which of the following statements about the 'notice of claim' condition in a standard health policy is correct?
o: Claims intimated late are automatically void
Cashless claims require no intimation
Intimation must be made only in writing by registered post
Delay in intimation or submission of documents may be condoned where the delay is proved to be for reasons beyond the insured's control
e: IRDAI requires insurers to condone delays due to circumstances beyond the insured's control; late intimation alone is not a valid ground for rejection.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: A policy covers pre-hospitalisation for 30 days and post-hospitalisation for 60 days. The insured was admitted on 10 March and discharged on 15 March. Which of the following expenses is admissible as pre-hospitalisation?
o: Consultation on 1 February for the same illness
Diagnostic tests on 20 February for the same illness
Physiotherapy on 20 April for the same illness
Dental check-up on 5 March for an unrelated problem
e: Pre-hospitalisation covers the 30 days before admission (9 February to 9 March) for the same condition; 1 February is outside the window, 20 April is post-hospitalisation and the dental visit is unrelated.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: 'Any one illness' in standard health policy wording means:
o: Every hospitalisation is treated as a separate illness
Only the first illness in the policy year
Continuous period of illness, including relapse within 45 days from the date of last consultation at the hospital/nursing home where treatment was taken
An illness lasting more than one year
e: The 45-day relapse rule links related admissions into one illness for the purpose of limits and sub-limits.

topic: Health Insurance Policy Forms and Clauses
t: Mr Rao's policy of ₹3 lakh has a cumulative bonus of ₹60,000 and the policy reduces cumulative bonus by 10% of base sum insured for every claim year. He makes a claim of ₹80,000 this year. At the next renewal, the sum insured including bonus will be:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Bonus of ₹60,000 is reduced by 10% of ₹3 lakh = ₹30,000, leaving ₹30,000; renewed cover = ₹3,00,000 + ₹30,000 = ₹3,30,000.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: Which of the following data items is LEAST useful for pricing a retail health product?
o: Age-wise claim frequency
Average length of stay and cost per hospitalisation
Medical inflation trend
The colour of the policy document
e: Pricing depends on exposure, frequency, severity and trend data; document design is irrelevant to cost.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: An insurer writes ₹120 crore of annual health premium evenly through the year. Using the 1/365th (pro-rata) method, the unearned premium reserve at year end would be approximately:
o: ₹30 crore
₹40 crore
₹60 crore
₹120 crore
e: Premium written evenly on annual policies is on average half unexpired at year end, so the reserve is about 50% of ₹120 crore = ₹60 crore.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: The 'loss ratio' most commonly used to assess the underwriting performance of a health portfolio is:
o: Claims paid divided by premium written
Outstanding claims divided by sum insured
Reinsurance recoveries divided by claims
Net incurred claims divided by net earned premium
e: Incurred claims (paid plus change in reserves) against earned premium matches claims to the period in which the premium was earned.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: Why is standardisation of hospital discharge summaries and billing formats important for health insurance data?
o: It helps insurers avoid paying claims
It is required by the Income-tax Act
It increases hospital tariffs
It allows consistent capture of diagnosis, procedure and cost fields, enabling analysis, fraud detection and faster claims processing
e: IRDAI and IIB have pushed standard formats so that claim data can be coded and compared across providers and insurers.

topic: Health Insurance Data, Pricing and Reserving
t: A health product priced at a 70% target loss ratio shows an actual incurred claims ratio of 95% after two years. The most appropriate actuarial response is:
o: Ignore it since health is short-tail
Load the premium only of those insureds who claimed
Stop paying claims above the target ratio
Review the pricing assumptions (frequency, severity, inflation, anti-selection) and file a revised premium for the product as a whole, along with underwriting and claims control measures
e: Persistent deviation requires re-pricing at product level with regulatory filing; selective individual loading is prohibited and claims must be paid as per contract.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, which of the following is an essential element for a health insurance contract to be valid?
o: The policy must be in Hindi
Registration with the sub-registrar
Offer and acceptance, consideration, competent parties, free consent and lawful object
Attestation by two witnesses
e: An insurance policy is a contract and must satisfy the general requirements of the Contract Act; the proposal is the offer, the premium the consideration.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Which of the following statements about IRDAI's regulation of health insurance products from 2024 is correct?
o: The IRDAI (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016 continue unchanged
Health insurance is now regulated by the Ministry of Health
Health products are now governed by the IRDAI (Insurance Products) Regulations, 2024 together with the Master Circular on Health Insurance Products issued in May 2024
Each State regulates health insurance separately
e: In 2024 IRDAI consolidated its product regulations and replaced numerous health circulars with a single Master Circular dated 29 May 2024.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: The maximum penalty that IRDAI can impose on an insurer for contravention of regulations (per instance) under the amended Insurance Act, 1938 is generally:
o: ₹5 lakh
₹25 lakh
₹1 crore
₹10 crore
e: Section 102 provides for penalties up to ₹1 crore for each failure to comply with the Act or regulations; certain other sections carry up to ₹25 crore.

topic: Claims timelines
t: For health insurance, the maximum time an insurer may take to decide a cashless authorisation request under the 2024 master circular is:
o: 1 hour
3 hours
6 hours
24 hours
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Cashless authorisation within 1 hour of request; final discharge authorisation within 3 hours.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Under the 2024 Master Circular, a policyholder who has made no claim during the policy year may be offered by the insurer:
o: A refund of full premium
Automatic conversion to a life policy
A choice of reward such as increased sum insured or a discount on premium (no claim bonus), as per product design
Waiver of all exclusions
e: No-claim benefits may be offered as cumulative bonus or premium discount; refunds of full premium are not a recognised reward.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: A hospital's bill includes charges for items under the 'optional items' list. Under IRDAI's standardisation guidelines, such items:
o: Must always be paid by the insurer
Are payable only if the product specifically covers them; otherwise they are to be borne by the insured
Are to be paid by the TPA
Are illegal for hospitals to charge
e: The standardised lists categorise items as not payable, payable subject to coverage or part of room/procedure charges; optional items are payable only when the policy covers them.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Mr Gupta (aged 45) pays ₹20,000 for his family's health policy, ₹4,000 for a preventive health check-up in cash, and ₹48,000 for his parents' (both above 60) policy. His total deduction under Section 80D is:
e: Self and family: ₹20,000 + ₹4,000 check-up = ₹24,000 (within ₹25,000; cash is allowed only for preventive check-up). Senior citizen parents: ₹48,000 (within ₹50,000). Total ₹72,000.

topic: Regulatory and Legal Aspects of Health Insurance
t: Which of the following statements about insurer-initiated premium revision for senior citizens is correct as per IRDAI's 2025 direction?
o: Premiums for senior citizens may be increased freely each year
Insurers should not increase premiums for policyholders aged 60 and above by more than 10% per annum without prior consultation with IRDAI
Senior citizen premiums are frozen for life
Senior citizen premiums must be reduced annually
e: In January 2025 IRDAI directed insurers to cap annual increases for senior citizens at 10% and to consult the Authority before exceeding it or withdrawing such products.

topic: Customer Service in Health Insurance
t: The purpose of a 'network hospital' or 'preferred provider network' is to:
o: Enable cashless treatment at pre-agreed tariffs, improving cost control and customer convenience
Restrict the insured's choice of doctors permanently
Replace reimbursement claims entirely
Avoid regulatory oversight
e: Network tie-ups allow direct settlement at negotiated rates; reimbursement at non-network hospitals usually remains available.

topic: Customer Service in Health Insurance
t: Under IRDAI's policyholder protection framework, an insurer must acknowledge a written grievance within:
o: Immediately or within 3 working days
15 days
30 days
45 days
e: Grievances must be acknowledged promptly (within 3 working days) with a reference number, and resolved within the stipulated period of 14 days under the 2024 norms.

topic: Health insurance norms
t: The maximum waiting period for pre-existing diseases in health insurance, after the 2024 IRDAI changes, is:
o: 24 months
36 months
48 months
60 months
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Reduced from 48 to 36 months; the moratorium period after which claims cannot be contested (except fraud) is 60 months.

topic: Customer Service in Health Insurance
t: An insured is unhappy that his reimbursement claim of ₹80,000 was settled at ₹65,000 and wants to escalate. The correct sequence of redressal is:
o: Ombudsman first, then the insurer
Insurer's grievance redressal officer, then Bima Bharosa/IRDAI grievance cell or the Insurance Ombudsman, and thereafter consumer forum or court if unresolved
Civil court first
Police complaint first
e: The grievance ladder starts with the insurer; the Ombudsman requires a prior representation to the insurer, and courts/consumer fora remain available as alternatives.

topic: Health Insurance Fraud
t: Which of the following is a policyholder-side fraud in health insurance?
o: A hospital inflating the number of ICU days
Concealing a pre-existing illness in the proposal to obtain cover
A TPA delaying authorisation
A reinsurer refusing a recovery
e: Non-disclosure of material health facts to obtain cover is misrepresentation by the policyholder; inflating ICU days is provider fraud.

topic: Health Insurance Fraud
t: 'Hard' fraud is best illustrated by:
o: Rounding up a genuine pharmacy bill
Forgetting to mention a minor past illness
Claiming the full room rent when the policy has a sub-limit
Fabricating a hospitalisation that never took place using forged bills and discharge papers
e: Hard fraud is deliberate fabrication of an event or documents; opportunistic padding of genuine claims is soft fraud.

topic: Health Insurance Fraud
t: A policy was purchased online on 2 January with a declared 'no illness'. On 25 January the insured is hospitalised for diabetic ketoacidosis with HbA1c of 11%, and records show insulin purchases in December. The most appropriate claims decision is:
o: Repudiate for non-disclosure of a pre-existing disease, with written reasons and the right of appeal, and consider cancellation of the policy for misrepresentation
Pay the claim because the policy was in force
Pay 50% under the moratorium rule
Refer the claim to the reinsurer for decision
e: Documentary evidence of treatment before inception establishes material non-disclosure within the moratorium period; the insurer may repudiate and act on the policy, following due process.

topic: Reinsurance
t: A reinsurance arrangement that pays the insurer when an individual claim exceeds a fixed amount (e.g. above ₹25 lakh on a large group policy) is called:
o: Per-risk excess of loss
Quota share
Stop loss
Surplus
e: Per-risk XL is non-proportional protection against individual large claims; stop-loss protects the aggregate loss ratio, and quota share/surplus are proportional.

topic: Reinsurance
t: 'Retrocession' means:
o: Return of premium to the insured
Reinsurance purchased by a reinsurer to pass on part of the risks it has accepted
Cancellation of a treaty
Commission paid to the broker
e: A reinsurer protects its own book by retroceding to other reinsurers; the retrocedant is the reinsurer and the retrocessionaire accepts the risk.

topic: Reinsurance
t: A health insurer has a stop-loss treaty attaching at 90% loss ratio with the reinsurer covering 90% of losses above that point up to 120%. Net earned premium is ₹500 crore and incurred claims are ₹550 crore. The reinsurer's payment is:
o: ₹50 crore
₹100 crore
₹90 crore
₹110 crore
e: Loss ratio is 110%; the excess over 90% is 20% × ₹500 crore = ₹100 crore; the reinsurer pays 90% of this = ₹90 crore, the cedant retaining 10% as co-participation.
